Follow-up with a more compact summary of the confirmed root cause and current local workaround.

I think the important distinction is that Desktop showing `~\playground` is only a display difference. The actual persisted records on Windows use the full backslash path:

```text
C:\Users\<user>\playground
```

The Web UI, however, can request the same project as:

```text
C:/Users/<user>/playground
```

When the session API filters by exact `directory` equality, those two strings do not match, so existing sessions are hidden even though they are still present in the database. In my local repro, querying the API with the backslash path returned the expected root sessions, while querying with the slash path returned none.

The smallest safe local workaround I found was to keep the OpenCode Web backend on localhost and place a tiny local proxy in front of it that normalizes Windows `directory` query parameters before forwarding. That avoids editing or rewriting the OpenCode database.

For future Windows reports, the repeatable diagnostic flow is:

1. Check the stored `project.worktree` and `session.directory` values in the OpenCode database.
2. Query the session API twice with the same project path, once as `C:\...` and once as `C:/...`.
3. If only the backslash form returns sessions, treat the database as intact and focus on server-side path normalization for the `directory` filter.
4. Avoid rewriting the database as a workaround; a local path-normalizing proxy is safer until the upstream API behavior is fixed.

The durable upstream fix still seems to be server-side normalization/equivalent matching for session/project directory filters, so API callers using either `C:\...` or `C:/...` resolve to the same project sessions.

This issue might be a duplicate of existing issues. Please check:
- #5474: `/undo` command only rolls back AI conversation message, not the associated file changes
- #4704: `/undo` and `/timeline` undo does not revert file edits

Your report adds a specific cross-repository scenario (changes in repo B not reverted when session is started in repo A), which may be a distinct edge case worth tracking separately. Please review the above issues and comment there if your situation is covered, or clarify how your case differs.

Thanks for checking and linking those issues.

I reviewed #5474 and #4704. They cover the more general case where `/undo` does not revert file edits, including cases within the active project/repository.

The distinction in this report is the repository boundary:

- opencode is started from Git repository `A`
- the assistant edits files in a separate Git repository `B`
- running `/undo` rolls back the conversation, but the changes in repository `B` remain

So this may be related to the same undo/snapshot mechanism, but the specific edge case is cross-repository edits made from a single session. If `/undo` is intentionally scoped only to the session's initial repository/worktree, then a warning or documentation note would address the safety issue. If it is intended to revert the last assistant turn regardless of which repository was modified, then repo `B` should probably be tracked as part of the undo state too.

Closing this from my side with the local resolution and the troubleshooting method that worked for me.

This should not be read as confirmation that the underlying Bun / TUI shutdown crash is fixed upstream. Other users may still hit the same bundled Bun 1.3.13 `NAPI FATAL ERROR` path, and the later comments here suggest there may be more than one trigger. In my case, the issue is no longer blocking my local OpenCode usage after isolating a local plugin/native dependency trigger.

## What the AI/agent investigation did

I used an OpenCode/AI-agent style investigation rather than trying random reinstall steps. The useful workflow was:

1. Capture the exact crash signature.
   - `panic: NAPI FATAL ERROR: Error::New napi_create_error`
   - `oh no: Bun has crashed`
   - `trace trap opencode`

2. Separate system Bun from bundled Bun.
   - My system `bun` was not the runtime used by OpenCode.
   - The OpenCode binary embedded `Bun v1.3.13`, so changing the system Bun version was not expected to fix this class of crash.

3. Narrow the reproduction surface.
   - Interactive TUI exit was the strongest signal.
   - `Ctrl + C`, `/exit`, and later reports of `/quit` all pointed at shutdown / teardown / cleanup behavior.
   - Non-interactive `opencode run ...` plus scripted SIGINT did not reproduce the same crash reliably for me.

4. Inspect OpenCode logs and macOS crash reports instead of only the terminal output.
   - OpenCode logs: `~/.local/share/opencode/log/`
   - macOS reports: `~/Library/Logs/DiagnosticReports/opencode-*.ips`

5. Compare OpenCode plugin loading with the local config.
   - I checked which plugins were configured and which ones were actually loaded.
   - I also checked plugin load failures and native modules present in the process.

6. Form one hypothesis at a time and verify it.
   - The strongest local evidence was not a normal JavaScript exception.
   - The macOS crash reports pointed at native dependency cleanup involving ONNX/WebGPU/sharp-related modules.

## Using OpenCode itself to investigate this kind of crash

The most useful part was letting an OpenCode/AI agent do the boring evidence collection and comparison, while explicitly instructing it not to jump to a reinstall or random fix.

A prompt that worked well for me was:

```text
Investigate this OpenCode crash systematically. Do not change files yet.

Goal:
Find whether the crash is caused by OpenCode itself, bundled Bun, my system Bun, a plugin, MCP config, or a local native dependency.

Crash signature:
<paste the full terminal crash output here>

Please:
1. Check opencode and system bun versions.
2. Determine whether OpenCode is using bundled Bun or system Bun.
3. Read recent OpenCode logs under ~/.local/share/opencode/log/.
4. Inspect macOS crash reports under ~/Library/Logs/DiagnosticReports/opencode-*.ips.
5. Identify native modules or symbols in the crash report.
6. Compare loaded plugins with ~/.config/opencode/opencode.jsonc and ~/.config/opencode/package.json.
7. Separate confirmed evidence from hypotheses.
8. Propose the smallest reversible fix first.
9. After any fix, verify with opencode --print-logs mcp list and opencode --print-logs models.
```

Useful commands for the agent to run:

```sh
opencode --version
which bun
bun --version
opencode --print-logs mcp list
opencode --print-logs models
```

Useful files/locations for the agent to inspect:

```text
~/.local/share/opencode/log/
~/.local/share/opencode/
~/.config/opencode/opencode.jsonc
~/.config/opencode/package.json
~/Library/Logs/DiagnosticReports/opencode-*.ips
```

What the agent should look for:

```text
- Whether the crash happens in interactive TUI only or also in opencode run
- Whether the latest log shows plugin load failures
- Whether crash reports mention native modules such as onnxruntime, sharp, libvips, sqlite, watcher, or other .node/.dylib files
- Whether a configured plugin pulls in native dependencies
- Whether disabling one plugin changes the result
- Whether a new op

Dynamic model discovery is the right approach for OpenAI-compatible gateways. Static model lists break the moment the gateway adds or removes models. Here's a pattern that works reliably across diverse backends:

**1. Probe `/v1/models` with graceful fallback**

```python
async def discover_models(base_url: str, api_key: str, timeout: float = 5.0) -> list[str]:
    """Discover available models from an OpenAI-compatible endpoint."""
    try:
        async with httpx.AsyncClient(timeout=timeout) as client:
            resp = await client.get(
                f"{base_url.rstrip('/')}/v1/models",
                headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {api_key}"}
            )
            if resp.status_code == 200:
                data = resp.json()
                return [m["id"] for m in data.get("data", [])]
    except (httpx.TimeoutException, httpx.ConnectError):
        pass
    return []  # Caller falls back to static list
```

**2. Cache with TTL and background refresh**

Model lists rarely change mid-session. Cache for 5-15 minutes with a background refresh:

```python
class ModelCache:
    def __init__(self, ttl_seconds=300):
        self._cache: dict[str, tuple[float, list[str]]] = {}
        self._ttl = ttl_seconds

    async def get_models(self, base_url, api_key) -> list[str]:
        key = base_url.rstrip("/")
        now = time.time()
        if key in self._cache:
            ts, models = self._cache[key]
            if now - ts < self._ttl:
                return models
        models = await discover_models(base_url, api_key)
        if models:
            self._cache[key] = (now, models)
        return models
```

**3. Capability inference from model IDs**

When the `/v1/models` response doesn't include capability metadata, infer from naming patterns:
- `*instruct*` -> chat/completion
- `*embed*` -> embeddings only
- `*vision*` or `*omni*` -> multimodal
- `*tts*` / `*whisper*` -> audio

This won't be perfect but handles 90% of real-world model names.

**4. Health check on startup**

Run a lightweight `/v1/models` probe when the provider is first configured and surface errors immediately in the UI rather than waiting for the first chat request to fail.

This pattern is what many multi-provider tools use (including gateway services) — it eliminates the "model not found" class of errors that users hit when gateways update their model catalog.

After the 5 hours quota reset:

# Confirmation after the reset

- The **continuous (5h) quota does reset**.
- The weekly and monthly quotas **do not** reset — they are cumulative and only decrease when their own cycle ends.

## Actual service capacity

| Concept | Value |
|---------|-------|
| Maximum per 5h window | $12.02 in API value |
| Total monthly pool | ~$61 |
| 5h windows supported per month | ~5 (the monthly pool runs out, not the 5h window) |
| Intensive usage hours per month | ~15h (5 windows × 3h each) |
| Days of 3h sessions | ~5 days, then 25 days without service |

## Comparison at 15h/month  
*(what you can actually use before the monthly quota breaks)*

| Service | $/month (15h) |
|---------|---------------|
| DeepSeek promo — only DS models (what you actually used) | $1.30 |
| DeepSeek promo — hypothetical if all traffic were DS | $3.51 |
| $10 subscription (flat rate, throttled) | $10.00 |
| DeepSeek without discount — only DS models | $15.91 |
| DeepSeek without discount — all traffic | $40.69 |
| OpenRouter (same catalog, no quotas) | $50.66 |

## Refined conclusion

- You will be able to use the service for **~15h per month** (5 intensive 3h sessions). For daily developer use, you'll be without service **25 days per month**.
- If you switch entirely to DeepSeek with the discount, you pay **$1.30/month** and get **unlimited access** (no quotas). But you lose **MiMo and GLM**.
- If you need MiMo/GLM, the subscription gives you a better price than OpenRouter ($10 vs $50), but with the **shackle of the 15h limit**.
